global.headline: IRAN — NEW SUPREME LEADER VOWS REVENGE FOR FATHER'S KILLING; TRUMP THREATENS TO "DECIMATE" IRAN OVER ASSASSINATION THREATS, EVEN AS TEHRAN PRIVATELY CALLS HORMUZ ATTACKS A "MISTAKE"
summary: Mojtaba Khamenei issued his first public statement since his father's funeral concluded, posting on X that Iran had compiled a list of individuals to be targeted over the 28 February strike that killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, saying "vengeance is the will of our nation and must inevitably be carried out." Hours earlier, Trump had threatened on Truth Social to "decimate and destroy" Iran if it acted on intelligence-flagged threats to assassinate him, writing that "1000 Missiles are Locked and Loaded and aimed at the Islamic Republic of Iran, with thousands of more to immediately follow," after mourners at Khamenei's funeral were seen carrying banners reading "We Will Kill Trump." The US Treasury separately sanctioned Dubai-based Iranian national Ali Ansari, accused of managing a global network of real estate and commercial holdings for Mojtaba Khamenei, other regime elites and the IRGC, alongside several Iranian exchange houses accused of moving billions of dollars for sanctioned banks through shell companies.

Even as the rhetoric escalated, US officials said Iranian representatives have privately acknowledged the 7 July attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz were a "mistake," carried out by an internal faction opposed to negotiations with Washington — and that Tehran wants talks to continue. Washington's immediate demand remains a public Iranian statement that all Hormuz shipping lanes are open and commercial vessels will not be targeted; Iran has not issued one, instead wanting to retain control of the strait and the ability to charge passing ships. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Omani counterpart Sayyid Badr Albusaidi in Muscat to discuss mechanisms for safe transit through the strait, part of the wider mediation push alongside Qatar and Pakistan.

Hormuz traffic remains well below the pre-war baseline of 120–140 crossings a day, moving mostly in naval-escorted convoys; war-risk insurance for tankers is pricing many multiples above pre-crisis levels and several P&I clubs have withdrawn cover. Mojtaba Khamenei's public re-emergence answers one open question from this arc — he is now visibly directing Iran's posture — but adds a fresh one: whether his revenge rhetoric is compatible with his own foreign ministry's parallel push to keep the MOU's remnants alive.
global.geopolitical: The new Supreme Leader publicly owning a revenge agenda, on the same day Washington escalates its own threats and adds fresh sanctions, narrows the room for the diplomatic track his own foreign minister is pursuing in Oman — a split-screen of vengeance and negotiation that mirrors the contradictory signals from the American side ("talks continue" alongside "ceasefire is over" and now missile threats).
global.socioeconomic: None of this has yet translated into a fresh oil-market shock or a reopened Hormuz — tanker traffic and insurance costs remain the practical chokepoint regardless of the rhetoric, and Singapore's downstream exposure (elevated electricity tariffs, softer tourism forecasts, stranded seafarers) stays unchanged until the strait's own numbers move, not the war of words above it.

global.headline: VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKE DEATH TOLL PASSES 4,300 AS RECOVERY EFFORT'S SCALE BECOMES CLEAR
summary: The Venezuelan government said Saturday the death toll from the back-to-back 7.5 and 7.2 magnitude earthquakes that struck the coastal state of La Guaira on 24 June has passed 4,300. Parliament chief Jorge Rodríguez wrote on Telegram that at least 4,333 people were killed and 16,740 injured, with thousands more still listed as missing more than two weeks after the quakes flattened entire districts. President Delcy Rodríguez and the United Nations have both issued fresh calls for international financial assistance as the scale of the recovery and rebuilding effort becomes clearer.
global.geopolitical: A death toll this size, still climbing more than two weeks on, puts renewed pressure on the international community's response to Venezuela — a government already navigating US sanctions and regional tensions — over how quickly aid and reconstruction financing materialise.
global.socioeconomic: Beyond the direct human toll, a disaster of this scale in a single coastal state implies years of rebuilding costs for housing, infrastructure and livelihoods in an economy with limited fiscal room, reinforcing why Caracas and the UN are now explicitly asking for outside financial help rather than absorbing the cost alone.

global.headline: FLOODS AND LANDSLIDES KILL AT LEAST 44 IN BANGLADESH, LEAVE OVER A MILLION STRANDED
summary: Days of torrential monsoon rain triggered floods and landslides across seven south-eastern Bangladesh districts — Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Bandarban, Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Habiganj — killing at least 44 people and stranding more than 267,000 households, over a million people in total. Power outages, damaged roads and severed communications have slowed rescue and relief work, and many residents have been unable to cook for days as floodwaters submerged homes or left kitchens and living spaces buried in mud. The rains also triggered landslides earlier in the week in the Rohingya refugee camps of Cox's Bazar, killing 16 refugees including women and children, on hillsides that are especially vulnerable to slope failure during monsoon season.
global.geopolitical: The Rohingya-camp deaths add a fresh layer of vulnerability for a refugee population of more than a million people already dependent on international humanitarian support, at a moment when Bangladesh's own disaster-response capacity is stretched by the wider flooding.
global.socioeconomic: As one of the world's most disaster-prone countries, Bangladesh faces a recurring seasonal calculus of flood damage, rebuilding cost and lost economic activity that scientists say climate change is intensifying — this event's toll and displacement scale are on the more severe end of that recurring pattern.

global.headline: TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SUBPOENAS FOUR NEW YORK TIMES JOURNALISTS OVER AIR FORCE ONE SECURITY REPORTING
summary: The Justice Department subpoenaed four New York Times journalists — Julian E. Barnes, Eric Lipton, Tyler Pager and Eric Schmitt — to testify before a federal grand jury in Manhattan next Wednesday, with federal agents delivering some subpoenas to reporters' homes. The move follows the Times's report earlier in the week that Trump left Turkey on the older Air Force One over Secret Service security concerns, after finding the newer, Qatari-gifted jet lacked some of the older plane's advanced security features, including antimissile capabilities. The subpoenas appear aimed at identifying who leaked to the paper before publication.

The Times said it will fight the grand jury order, calling it a direct threat to the press's ability to gather information in the public interest; press-freedom advocacy groups condemned the subpoenas as an attack on the public's right to know about government operations. The Justice Department defended the action, saying reporters are not the targets — those who leaked classified information are.
global.geopolitical: Subpoenaing journalists rather than pursuing the leak through other means is an unusually aggressive posture even by the standards of prior US leak investigations, and will be read internationally as a signal of how far the administration is willing to go against domestic media over national-security reporting.
global.socioeconomic: A protracted legal fight over reporter subpoenas creates a chilling precedent for national-security journalism generally, regardless of this case's outcome — sources who would otherwise flag safety or security lapses have one more reason to stay silent.

global.headline: LANDMARK US HOUSING AFFORDABILITY BILL BECOMES LAW WITHOUT TRUMP'S SIGNATURE
summary: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act — described as the most comprehensive US housing legislation in decades, aimed at increasing supply and curbing costs including limits on institutional investors buying up single-family homes — became law automatically at midnight Friday into Saturday after Trump declined to either sign or veto it. Trump had said on Truth Social he would withhold his signature "in PROTEST" over the Senate's failure to pass the separate SAVE America Act, an elections bill. Because the bill had been sitting with the White House since 29 June, the constitutional clock ran out and it took effect without presidential action.
global.geopolitical: A bipartisan Congress effectively overriding a president's objection through inaction rather than a veto override is a notable, if procedural, assertion of legislative will against Trump on a domestic priority, distinct from the more usual congressional deference on his other agenda items.
global.socioeconomic: Substantively, the law's institutional-investor limits and supply-side measures are aimed squarely at the kind of affordability pressure Singapore policymakers are separately grappling with in the HDB resale and EC markets — a reminder that housing-cost politics are running hot across very different systems at the same time.

singapore.headline: BARISAN NASIONAL WINS JOHOR STATE ELECTION IN A LANDSLIDE, WIPING OUT PERIKATAN NASIONAL
summary: Barisan Nasional won a two-thirds-plus majority in Saturday's Johor state election, securing 48 of 56 seats — Umno took 36 of the 37 seats it contested, MCA won 8 of 15, and MIC swept all 4 it contested. Pakatan Harapan took the remaining 8 seats (6 DAP, 1 Amanah, 1 PKR), while Perikatan Nasional, Bersama and Muda were wiped out entirely. Malaysia's immigration authorities had set up a special taskforce and dedicated lanes at Singapore-Johor checkpoints to manage voting-day crossings, reflecting how many Johoreans commute into Singapore for work.
singapore.geopolitical: A decisive BN win preserves the pragmatic, investment-friendly political continuity that Singapore and foreign investors have been counting on for the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and the Rapid Transit System Link, removing — at least for this electoral cycle — the uncertainty a stronger nationalist-bloc showing would have injected into cross-border planning.
singapore.socioeconomic: For Singaporeans increasingly treating Johor Bahru as a cost-of-living hedge for housing, groceries and leisure, a stable and continuity-minded state government is the more favourable outcome, reducing the odds of policy disruption to the cross-border arrangements many are informally relying on.

singapore.headline: AT LEAST 20 FLIGHTS FROM SINGAPORE CANCELLED AS TYPHOON BAVI HITS JAPAN, THEN MAKES LANDFALL IN CHINA
summary: At least 20 flights out of Changi Airport were cancelled as Typhoon Bavi swept past Japan and approached Taiwan and China, with passengers advised to check the Changi Airport website for updates. Bavi went on to make landfall in the coastal city of Yuhuan, Zhejiang province, at around 11.20pm local time Saturday, with maximum sustained winds of 144kph. Chinese authorities evacuated more than 1.7 million people ahead of the storm — over half a million in Zhejiang and more than 100,000 in neighbouring Fujian — with hundreds of flights cancelled and rail and ferry services suspended across the affected provinces.
singapore.geopolitical: None material — a weather event, though the scale of China's evacuation response (1.7 million people) illustrates the disaster-preparedness capacity Beijing can mobilise on short notice.
singapore.socioeconomic: Beyond the immediate Changi disruption, a storm of this scale moving through China's east coast typically has knock-on effects for regional shipping and air-cargo schedules that Singapore's trade- and logistics-dependent economy will likely feel over the coming days as flight and port schedules normalise.

singapore.headline: HDB: ONE IN THREE EC INCOME-CEILING WAIVER APPEALS APPROVED SINCE 2020, AS SANDWICH-CLASS BUYERS PUSH BACK ON THE $16,000 CAP
summary: HDB data released Saturday show more than 2,500 appeals were filed from 2020 to 2025 by executive condominium buyers seeking a waiver of the household income ceiling, currently set at $16,000 a month; 845 of those appeals, roughly one in three, were approved. The figures put a number on a long-running sandwich-class complaint — that dual-income professional households can exceed the EC income cap while still finding private property out of reach, leaving the appeals channel as their main route into the EC segment.
singapore.geopolitical: None material — a domestic housing-policy data release.
singapore.socioeconomic: A roughly one-in-three approval rate suggests the ceiling is a real, binding constraint rather than a formality for a meaningful slice of sandwich-class households, feeding into the same affordability conversation already in this briefing via the first HDB resale-price decline since 2019 and record COE premiums.

singapore.headline: WHATSAPP LOCKS DOWN USERNAMES OF SINGAPORE POLITICIANS AHEAD OF NEW PRIVACY FEATURE, TO PRE-EMPT IMPERSONATION
summary: Ahead of a wider rollout of WhatsApp usernames — a privacy feature that lets users hide their phone numbers — Meta has already locked down usernames tied to senior Singapore politicians including Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, Health Minister Ong Ye Kung and Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan, along with lookalike variations such as @LawrenceW0ng and @Lawrence_Wong. Checks found usernames for Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong and Home Affairs Minister K Shanmugam were similarly unavailable. Meta said the reservations are meant to let legitimate owners claim the names later and to reduce impersonation risk for high-profile public figures.
singapore.geopolitical: None material — a platform-level security measure.
singapore.socioeconomic: The pre-emptive lockdown is a direct response to the same impersonation-and-scam risk this briefing has repeatedly tracked via SPF's moneylending and fraud crackdowns — a sign platforms are starting to build in guardrails against political-figure impersonation before a feature ships, rather than patching it after abuse appears.

word.definition: A prolonged, bitter feud or campaign of revenge pursued between individuals, families or factions over a perceived wrong, often carried on across generations.
word.etymology: From Italian vendetta ("revenge, blood feud"), from Latin vindicta ("vengeance, act of vindication"), from vindicare ("to lay legal claim to, to avenge"). Entered English through 19th-century accounts of Corsican and Sicilian blood feuds, later generalised to any implacable, personal campaign of retaliation.
word.example: Mojtaba Khamenei's first public words since his father's funeral were not a policy statement but a vendetta pledge — a target list and a vow that "vengeance... must inevitably be carried out" — delivered the same day his own foreign minister sat down in Oman to talk about keeping the Strait of Hormuz open.
